title: Similarity and normalisation
outcome: By the end, I can explain similarity and normalisation using a traced example and a stated limitation.
scenario: Compare angular alignment with raw distance on the same vectors.
given: Query [2, 0]; P=[8, 0]; Q=[2, 1]. Nonzero vectors only; compare squared Euclidean distance and cosine.
All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

steps.label: Raw distances
steps.detail: P distance36; Q distance1, so Q is closer in raw coordinates.

steps.label: Angular similarity
steps.detail: CosineP=1; cosineQ=2/sqrt5≈0.8944, so P aligns more closely.

steps.label: Normalise
steps.detail: Unit query [1, 0], P [1, 0], Q [2/sqrt5, 1/sqrt5]; normalised distanceP0.

explanation: Raw Euclidean distance includes differences in both direction and magnitude. Cosine compares direction using the vector lengths, so a long vector can align perfectly while being far away in raw coordinates. Declare which question your similarity measure answers. A zero vector has no direction and cannot be divided by its norm for cosine or unit normalisation.

counterfactual.prediction: Cosine and unit normalisation for P are undefined.
counterfactual.reason: The zero vector has norm0, so dividing by its norm is invalid.

student_task: Why do the original two metrics select different winners? Point to the relevant step in the picture, then write the changed result and the rule or evidence that supports it.
teacher_answer: Raw distance includes length differences; cosine compares direction after accounting for norms. P shares direction but has a much larger magnitude. Changed-case check: Cosine and unit normalisation for P are undefined. The zero vector has norm0, so dividing by its norm is invalid.
project_evidence: For your Image-pattern Network Investigation, save the input, procedure, observed result and limitation of this check. Label this worked example as practice; use a different, previously unreviewed case when checking independent understanding.
limits: Neither metric is universally right; choose it from the task and handle zero vectors explicitly.
